HEADLINE: Turnbull hires venture capital pioneer Ferris to drive innovation economy
INTRO: Veteran venture capitalist Bill Ferris will spearhead the Turnbull government's innovation agenda that will use tax breaks and greater cooperation between business and CSIRO to drive technology companies and start ups.
TEXT:
Veteran venture capitalist Bill Ferris will spearhead the Turnbull government's innovation agenda that will use tax breaks and greater cooperation between business and CSIRO to drive technology companies and start ups.

As the innovation czar, Mr Ferris will advise Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, Treasurer Scott Morrison and industry, innovation and science Minister Christopher Pyne how to make technology, innovation and start-ups a new pillar of the economy.

The government will release a landmark innovation statement early next month with a broad agenda covering changes to tax, research and development incentives, university funding and the role of CSIRO.

CSIRO is preparing to launch its own venture capital fund drawing on its $450 million Wi-Fi patent windfall, of which up to $100 million remains.

The research agency's fund will help the government achieve its goal of getting more from its $9.7 billion in annual research spending by providing stronger incentives for researchers, investors and industry to collaborate and turn ideas into businesses.

The appointment of Mr Ferris, who is co-chairman of CHAMP Private Equity and a former chairman of Austrade, will be announced next month. He declined to comment on the job but said Mr Turnbull "has got this tiger by the tail. Leadership can create momentum, and he is doing so."

A founder of Australia's private equity industry, he was chosen as one of the 50 most influential people in Australian business by The Australian Financial Review over the past half century. "It's not just about start-ups, although that is a phase of the innovation process where we can do a heap more and should do a heap more," he said.

Australia lags other rich countries in commercialising research - or turning it into businesses - according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the World Economic Forum.

Greg Clark, a former chief executive of US satellite company Loral and executive of Rupert Murdoch's 21st Century Fox, said the goal should be to exploit developments in micro-electronics. "That is, chips technology and software advancements over the past 30 years," he said.

Mr Pyne told industry representatives this week the innovation statement will include tax changes, a bigger role for CSIRO in funding commercialisation, and a shift in university funding to reward closer engagement with industry and start-ups.

Industry sources said Mr Pyne had described three pillars to the innovation agenda, led by a broad review of the tax system - not just a "tweaking" - "to prime the innovation and start-up culture".

Changes to research and development tax concessions, relaxing capital-raising rules to allow "crowdfunding" from retail investors through the internet, expanding tax breaks for angel investors in new start-ups, and copying hi-tech leaders like Israel and Singapore that subsidise employment in innovation, are all possible.

The policy would also include a bigger role for CSIRO in forging closer ties between researchers and business and in funding commercialisation and start-ups, a direction in which chief executive and former entrepreneur Larry Marshall is already taking the agency.

The third pillar would be a change to make universities and academics' funding dependent on engaging with industry and successfully creating start-ups from their research.

In Britain up to a fifth of university funding is dependent on engagement with industry, which must be substantiated by case studies.

These changes could include changes to academic pay and promotions criteria to shift incentives away from publishing for its own sake and towards start-ups and industry collaboration.

CSIRO's proposed venture capital fund will draw on the remainder of the research agency's $450 million windfall from protracted worldwide patent litigation over the use of Wi-Fi technology, which was invented by John O'Sullivan, a scientist at the agency.

CSIRO fund will join new venture capital funds that could total $1 billion by the middle of next year as the nation's universities, investment managers and superannuation funds get behind the push to create a stronger innovation ecosystem.

However, a Turnbull Government facing a parlous fiscal position will insist the cost of changes to innovation funding and taxes must be balanced by revenue increases, such as a possible increase in the GST.

This suggests major alterations in the tax code will be delayed until after the next election.

Mr Ferris said the challenge for the government is to deal with "a national budget that needs some rebalancing and at the same time to shift the culture and the economy into one that really wants to commercialise new things and new discoveries". "To do that with a zero sum box of dollars will be very challenging," he said.

Mr Ferris, who started his first hi-tech investment company in Australia in 1970 after graduating from Harvard Business School, will influence much of the new policy direction.

He said building a strong innovation system would require a cultural shift starting with young people and seeing it develop "in digital business models and web-based app models".

He said there was "a huge challenge" in small and medium firms "where many thousands of companies can do a lot better" in harnessing innovation without becoming billion-dollar companies.

Mr Ferris said there are 20,000 Australians in Silicon Valley and elsewhere and it was important that "our best and brightest" have offshore experience.

"But we should try and attract them to do innovation work in Australia, because it attracts the suppliers and other jobs," he said.

Michelle Deaker, partner in venture capital firm One Ventures and SevenWest media director, said hi-tech firms now feel the innovation economy will have government support and there had already been a lot more investment activity.

While an internet start-up is automatically a "global business," Dr Deaker said local firms could tap bigger markets, job pools and professional networks by moving overseas.

HEADLINE: Australia Post plans drone delivery
INTRO: Trial is part of a move towards smart practices.
TEXT:
Trial is part of a move towards smart practices.

A trial of parcel deliveries by drone will be kicked off by Australia Post next year.

Chief executive Ahmed Fahour told AFR Weekend drones were not gimmicks and the company had already begun testing deliveries using the new technology.

"We've been talking to a major customer, an e-tailer, who would like to particularly deliver to regional and rural communities," Mr Fahour said.

"How do you get the parcel they've bought [from the] street to their home? We're focused on convenience. So we're going to trial in 2016 with a major customer."

Mr Fahour said a drone could hold parcels weighing up to two kilograms.

"It meets all of the flying requirements, has backup engines, GPS co-ordinates, so we can put it right on their patio," he said.

"It's the thin edge of trying to demonstrate that when you think of Australia Post - they're innovative. We're hopefully trying to show with the lockers [for parcel pick up], the app, that we are innovative."

Mr Fahour said the drones were just one example of innovation the business was looking at.

He said the company was also looking at having 3D printers available at Post Offices.

"Some things you want, like household items, could be printed right there and then rather than waiting for it," Mr Fahour said. "This is the new world, the technological revolution as opposed to the industrial revolution."

He said 2 million Australians have already signed up to My Post, which enables customers to pay bills, use the Australia Post app and even nominate a 24 hour locker for parcels to be collected from.

Just this week American retail giant Wal-mart announced they had begun testing drone delivery capabilities.

On Friday, Australia Post launched a $20 million innovation capital fund, expected to grow to $100 million, which will run in conjunction with the University of Melbourne.

The fund will be operated by Australia Post Accelerator, which will be independent of the company's core business.

"We're doing this to avoid the corporate "innovator's dilemma" whereby good ideas are either too small and they get swamped by other priorities or they are smothered by corporate protocols," Mr Fahour said.

"Our Accelerator will not be involved in creating inventions itself. Our Accelerator will be focused on innovation, which is the commercialisation of inventions."

Mr Fahour said Australia Post staff would be based at the university and would be tasked with the brief of developing "tangible commercial venture opportunities in the eCommerce market".

"We're specifically looking for entrepreneurs with an idea that aligns with our strategic focus of growing the Australian eCommerce market. We will also sponsor a scholarship at the Wade Institute of Entrepreneurship at Ormond College."

Melbourne University is expected to be the first of many hubs for Australia Post to grow its innovation capabilities.

"We will [collaborate with] other universities, we want to work with government, the CSIRO and we want to be part of really accelerating what Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has talked about. Take advantage of this digital disruption and don't become the loser of it. We have a unique opportunity and can actually prosper."

Australia Post has suffered setbacks with a decline in their letter business in the last seven years but remains one of the most trusted companies.

"If we only do what we have been doing recently, then as the letter goes down, the usage, then so do we," he said. "As Australians become more digitally aware, we want to change with them."

HEADLINE: Shorten plan to reduce voting age to 16
INTRO: Australia's minimum voting age could be as young as 16 under a Labor election plan to target Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's greatest electoral weakness, the youth vote.
TEXT:
Australia's minimum voting age could be as young as 16 under a Labor election plan to target Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull's greatest electoral weakness, the youth vote.

In a 21st century take on the 250-year-old political slogan, "no taxation without representation", Labor leader Bill Shorten will argue teenagers are already active participants in public life, and 17,000 teenagers pay $41 million a year in tax but have no say in their political representation.

The lower voting age will dovetail with Labor's key election messages, particularly that a Coalition government will reduce penalty rates, reduce job security, and slash education funding - all issues that disproportionately affect young Australians.

Scotland, Austria, Germany, Norway, Switzerland, the Philippines, Argentina, Nicaragua, Brazil and Ecuador have already lowered the voting age to 16 in national or local elections, which has triggered predictions of a new global trend to lower voting ages, similar to the Vietnam War-era trend of the 1970s that saw the voting age in many countries fall from 21 to 18 years.

For those parents who cannot trust their teenagers to clean their own rooms, let alone be part of the democratic process, Labor will remind older voters that Australia already trust teenagers to hold firearms licences, fly planes, and even pilot hot-air balloons.

Under Australian laws, 16 and 17-year-olds are allowed to join the military, drive on roads and make independent decisions about their health.

Last year, Scottish 16 and 17-year-olds voted in the Scottish independence referendum. A similar change in Australia could have ramifications for referendums and plebiscites, including same-sex marriage, Indigenous constitutional recognition, and the republic. It could affect the way political campaigns are conducted considering many young people say their political views are shaped by 140-character tweets and friends' Facebook likes.

Mr Turnbull appointed the youngest ever minister since the 1901 Federation when he made 25-year-old Wyatt Roy the assistant Minister for Innovation. But Labor still has a stranglehold on the youth vote which was a powerful weapon in the Kevin '07 campaign.

Labor dominates in the 18 to 24 and the 25 to 34-year-old age brackets, leading 51.5 per cent to the Coalition's 48.5 per cent, shows a Morgan Poll on October 19.

Despite Mr Turnbull's pitch of optimism and embracing the digital age, opinion polls show his greatest problem is convincing young people to support the Liberal-National party.

Labor will focus on building a greater young voter turnout at the next federal election which could prove a boon in marginal seats considering the fact 400,000 Australians who turned 18 between 2010 and 2013 did not enrol to vote. Voters put their trust in their parliamentary representatives so parliaments "have to trust the people they serve", Mr Shorten will tell a young Labor event on Saturday.

"This is why I want Australia to think about lowering the voting age, to give more young Australians a say.

"I believe young people want to be involved in decision-making processes and should be offered the opportunity to do so within our existing structure."

Key points

Bill Shorten says since 17,000 teens pay $41m in tax they should have representation.

Other countries have lowered the voting age, indicating a global trend.

HEADLINE: Criminal charge no bar to recompense
INTRO: A butcher's apprentice sacked after being arrested on charges of being an accessory after the fact to murder has been compensated for unfair dismissal
TEXT:
A butcher's apprentice sacked after being arrested on charges of being an accessory after the fact to murder has been compensated for unfair dismissal

The Fair Work Commission heard the apprentice's mood and appearance at work deteriorated in the weeks leading up his arrest in 2014 on the serious criminal charges.

"[The apprentice] received a phone call at work. A short time later I noticed him sharpening his knife very aggressively and I said to him, 'What's up?' and he replied by saying, 'If any of them touch me mates, I will stab them'," a co-worker told the commission.

The apprentice's employer, a NSW meat supplier, said the apprentice did not attend work on September 22, 2014 because he was in custody. He said he sacked him days later, fearing other employees would resign and customers would boycott the retail butcher store if he remained at work.

In a ruling this week, senior deputy president Jonathan Hamberger said he accepted that the employer believed the apprentice's actions were serious enough to justify immediate dismissal.

But he found "on the balance of probabilities" the employer had a "knee-jerk reaction" to the news the apprentice had been charged, fuelled by reports of customer and employee dissatisfaction.

He said the apprentice, who remains on bail, was not at work at the time the actions that led to his criminal charge occurred.

"While it is not the case that out-of-hours conduct can never be a valid reason for dismissing an employee, the starting point must be that what an employee does on his or her own time is a matter for him or her," he said.

"There is no presumption that a criminal conviction alone is a valid reason for termination of employment, particularly where the criminal offence was committed outside of work. Even conduct outside of work involving criminal offences does not, alone, warrant dismissal.

"There must still be a relevant connection between the criminal activity and the employee's employment."

While the unusual combination of circumstances combined to give the employer a valid reason to dismiss the apprentice, it did not afford him procedural fairness in effecting the dismissal.

The commission ruled out reinstatement and awarded compensation of six weeks' wages.

HEADLINE: ANZ sacks two more traders
INTRO: ANZ Banking Group has revealed that it has dismissed two more traders that were placed under suspension as a result of a regulatory probe into potential manipulation of the market's key bank bill swap rate.
TEXT:
ANZ Banking Group has revealed that it has dismissed two more traders that were placed under suspension as a result of a regulatory probe into potential manipulation of the market's key bank bill swap rate.

The bank has now dismissed three of the seven traders it initially placed under suspension a year ago as the Australian Securities and Investment Commission explored the bank's conduct in trading the rate which is used to set billions of dollars of securities and is a key determinant of lending rates.

The dismissals, the bank said, were not related to market trading practices that are the subject of the probe. Rather the sackings related to breaches of the bank's code of conduct relating to the use of systems, equipment and information policies. The traders are understood to have been informed in recent weeks.

"ANZ takes compliance with this policy very seriously and does not tolerate employees who use grossly offensive language and make disparaging comments about women or people generally on ANZ's systems," the bank said in a statement.

Some of the traders, mostly men, held senior positions on the bank's trading floor and managed the bank's balance sheet positions. ANZ said it did not comment on individual staff members.

Another major bank is also understood to have also sacked a short term rates trader for conduct breaches not related to the BBSW investigation.

In November 2014, ANZ stood down seven traders on full pay as the regulator stepped up its intense investigation into potential manipulation of the bank bill swap rate.

Three foreign banks - BNP Paribas, Royal Bank of Scotland and UBS - have agreed to enforceable undertakings but so far the ANZ suspensions have been the only action taken by a major banks. An ASIC report said benchmark rates were manipulated to increase the value of positions held by a certain bank, to trigger stop losses among clients and force them into losses, by sharing confidential client information and submitting low rates to force down an institution's cost of funding.

The investigation into rate rigging was understood to have been prompted by international intelligence gathered by offshore regulatory bodies that were exploring manipulation of global interest rates.

ASIC chair Greg Medcraft said earlier this month the complex investigation was ongoing and foreign banks had proved more cooperative than domestic banks on the issue because they have "often been through this in their own jurisdictions."

HEADLINE: Turnbull opens door to more Gonski funding
INTRO: Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has signalled his government will consider the student-based funding model recommended by the Gonski review but any commitment to fund the promised $7 billion in the final two years of the eduction package would have to take account of the tight federal budget position.
TEXT:
Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has signalled his government will consider the student-based funding model recommended by the Gonski review but any commitment to fund the promised $7 billion in the final two years of the eduction package would have to take account of the tight federal budget position.

As Labor ramps up its attack on the Coalition's education funding credentials, Mr Turnbull has stepped back from his predecessor Tony Abbott's opposition to the $14.5 billion Gonski model which five state and territory government signed in 2013 with the then Labor government.

The so-called Gonski funding for NSW, South Australia, Tasmania, Victoria and the ACT began in 2014 for an intended six years but after the 2013 election the Abbott government said it would renegotiate the agreement for the final two years of funding.

While the Coalition had promised to match the original funding amount, it had not promised to use the Gonski model to distribute it and Labor's attacks over the ambiguity of the future of federal education funding is gaining traction as the 2016 pre-election budget looms.

Mr Turnbull was in Tasmania on Friday speaking to Tasmanian premier Will Hodgeman about the state's 40 per cent Year 12 drop-out rate and suggested the federal government was focused on using the education funding to improve teacher quality, instead of other Gonski recommendations such as reducing class sizes.

He also countered Labor attacks that the Coalition had cut education funding, saying the previous Labor government did not provide funding for the final two years of the Gonski package.

"They talked about it but they didn't allow the funding for it. So there are big challenges with every aspect of the budget given the deficit situation we're in," Mr Turnbull said.

"This is all being considered by the Government in the context of a very tight Budget. Let me just say to you that the federal support for education right across the board is increasing and it will increase in the future."

Mr Turnbull said his education minister, Simon Birmingham, would have more to say on funding shortly.

While the Coalition has been criticised for the perception of a broken 2013 election promise on matching Labor for education funding, the previous Labor government has also been criticised for failing to provide funding the final two years of policy beyond that contained in a press release.

Labor leader Bill Shorten said the status of education and teaching had slipped backwards in Australia over the past three decades and young teachers needed to be encouraged to stay in the profession.

"We call upon Malcolm Turnbull to stop having thought bubbles about education, nice pleasant after-dinner conversations, and instead get on with the business of keeping the promise that was made at the last election so that all kids in all schools can know that they will be funded according to their needs and teachers are able to do the best they can possibly do, giving our kids the best start in life," he said.

HEADLINE: Inflation targeting still works: 'shadow' RBA
INTRO: Several members of a prominent Reserve Bank of Australia "shadow board" have weighed in on growing criticism of central banks world wide for trying to reignite inflation.
TEXT:
Several members of a prominent Reserve Bank of Australia "shadow board" have weighed in on growing criticism of central banks world wide for trying to reignite inflation.

According to former Morgan Stanley Asia chairman Stephen Roach global monetary policy, led by the US Federal Reserve, has been turned from a driver of price stability to "an engine of financial instability".

He accuses central banks of fighting the "wrong war" by cutting interest rates and printing money in an effort to get inflation rates up and avoid deflation. A surge in financial risks caused by ultra easy monetary policy means interest rates should now be increased.

Writing in The Australian Financial Review this week Mr Roach likened today's central bankers to the British army in the Battle of Singapore in 1942, where defences ensconced in bunkers facing the sea were useless against a Japanese attack from inland.

"Inflation targeting was once essential to limit runaway price growth," Mr Roach wrote. "In today's inflation-less world, however, it is counterproductive."

But several members of an RBA shadow board - a university group of experts that critiques central bank policy - have weighed in as Reserve Bank board prepares to meet on Tuesday, with financial markets anticipating a near-50 per cent chance of another official interest rate cut.

Bob Gregory, a former Reserve Bank board member and one of Australia's most experienced central bankers, doesn't share that view, even if he agrees that interest rates should be higher.

"Central banks are not at all worried about [spurring] inflation," he says. "They're focused on output growth and employment."

He says the current dilemma about interest rates is the same one that confronted policy-makers in the 1930s. "If you're as old as I am, you remember there was a time in the Great Depression when it was a common belief that monetary policy wouldn't generate jobs," he told AFR Weekend.

"It was the old 'pushing on a string argument' and we're now back to thinking about that lesson, which is that monetary policy can't do the job for you.

"The question becomes where do you turn? To fiscal policy? Most countries don't want to go down that path because they have a deficit overhang."

Another member of the Australian National University's shadow RBA board member, UNSW business school economist James Morley, who has worked at banks in the US, Canada and New Zealand, sees no good argument for dropping inflation targeting as the primary tool of monetary policy.

"Inflation targeting has been remarkably successful compared to any other monetary policy regime we've seen. The issue of financial stability is something that requires different instruments and tools," he says of Mr Roach's argument that rates should be hiked to reduce asset price risk.

Professor Morley adds that former Fed chairman Ben Bernanke learnt the lesson of the Great Depression, which is that you don't want to over react to fears about financial stability.

"Things would have been worse if, after the financial crisis, the Fed had moved away from an inflation targeting framework and ended up targeting asset prices and raised rates at the wrong time," he said.

By contrast, Mark Crosby, another shadow board member and associate professor in economics at Melbourne University's business school, agrees with Mr Roach's criticism. "If the economy isn't doing well with interest rates at 2 per cent, surely monetary policy isn't the problem," he said.

Professor Crosby opposed a rate cut..

HEADLINE: Packed hotels resort to pop-up container rooms
INTRO: The lower Australian dollar is boosting tourism.
TEXT:
The lower Australian dollar is boosting tourism.

Two 20-foot shipping containers masquerading as a luxury hotel suite, including a rooftop jacuzzi and terrace, will soon be floating on Sydney harbour for two nights.

If the visuals of the mining boom were all about trucks and railway trains carting the black gold, the hotel boom is cranes, scaffolding, lavish openings - and the odd quirky pop-up suite as hoteliers get crafty about wowing their clientele.

"There's a real trend towards the thrilling and off-beat," says Stefan Cordiner, from hotel booking app HotelTonight, which has partnered with Ovolo Hotels to create the "Spontaneity Suite", a pop-up hotel room made from two shipping containers dropped into scenic locations across Australia and raising money for charity OzHarvest.

Pop-ups like the spontaneity suite - and St Jerome's in Melbourne (20 luxury safari-style tents on level three of Melbourne Central mall available through until May 2016) - are appearing as Australia enjoys its best hotel market conditions in decades, with inner city occupancy rates surging above 80 per cent and thousands of new hotel rooms in the pipeline in Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane and Adelaide according the latest Savills Hotels Market Report.

Hotel returns are rising on the back of the tourism boom as record numbers of overseas visitors, many from Asia, take advantage of the lower Australian dollar to visit for holidays, work or to see family.

Sydney's occupancy rate hit 86 per cent in September, according to hotel market researchers STR Global, a record for that month, while the average room rate of $195 a night was second only to the September of the Sydney Olympics in 2000.

"Australia's burgeoning tourism industry has never been more important for our economy, especially for cities like Brisbane and Perth, which have experienced softening in occupancy due to the slowdown in the mining sector," said Simon McGrath, chief operating Officer at Accor Hotels Pacific, the biggest hotel operator in Australia with brands like the Pullman and Sofitel in its vast portfolio.

"Sydney and Melbourne are still the top performing markets for AccorHotels and the luxury hotel sector is seeing some of its strongest growth since 2008."

With China arrivals set to double from 100 million to 200 million by 2020, McGrath said it was "imperative we keep on top of our luxury product and continue to innovate".

Over the next two years, Accor has more than 3,000 rooms coming online in Australia, of which half are new build luxury developments like Sofitel Darling Harbour, Sofitel Adelaide and MGallery Elements of Byron Resort.

In Sydney, Singapore hotel tycoon Michael Kum is catering for the rising demand for accommodation by adding 222 rooms as part of a new 25-level tower atop the Four Points by Sheraton Sydney hotel overlooking Darling Harbour. Another hotel magnate, Jerry Schwartz is building two floors above the Rydges Sydney Central hotel, where occupancy rates have soared above 90 per cent.

Schwartz will also take ownership of the new $340 million, Accor-managed Sofitel Sydney Darling Harbour Hotel, when it's completed in 2017.

Melbourne is the other standout performer, particularly in the five-star luxury hotel segment, with occupancy at all almost 90 per cent, according to STR Global and average room rates up eight per cent over the year to date to $302 a night. Casino billionaire James Packer has been heavily promoting a new 90 storey high-rise tower at Crown Melbourne incorporating 388 hotel rooms - while still seeking approval for his proposed $2 billion Crown casino and hotel complex at Sydney's Barangaroo.

Earlier this month, a Singaporean developer won approval to build a 56-level hotel above Little Lonsdale Street in Melbourne; elsewhere in the city, construction is under way on a new Ritz-Carlton, a Four Points by Sheraton Hotel and Amalgamated Holding's QT Melbourne.

Even in Perth, where the tapering off of the mining boom has reduced demand for hotel rooms during the week, the overall occupancy rate remains above 80 per cent with average room rates still high at $198 a night.

New hotels confirmed for Perth include two DoubleTree hotels by Hilton Worldwide and a new Ritz-Carlton as part of the Elizabeth Quay project.

In Brisbane, occupancy rates at five-star hotels remain above 80 per cent despite a flood of new hotel openings before last year's G20 Summit. The city's signature hotel project is the 1100 room Ritz-Carlton planned for Echo Entertainment's $2 billion Queen's Wharf Casino project with construction to begin in 2017.

"There's a sense of optimism in Queensland, with the tourism industry telling us it's the best it's been before the GFC," Tourism and Events Queensland CEO, Leanne Coddington told AFR Weekend.

The hotel boom has also spread into Adelaide, a city starved until recently of new hotels, with half a dozen new projects under way, including a new Aloft hotel to be operated by US giant Starwood alongside new hotels by Choice, Accor and Intercontinental Hotels.

If you prefer something more quirky, head for The Frames, a recently opened resort in SA's Riverland wine growing region, featuring three architecturally designed retreats with huge spa rooms and designer pools.

Adding a touch of luxury to The Murray river, they also offer private cruises to a boutique brewery.

HEADLINE: Insurers wary of cut to rebate
INTRO: Health funds have warned their minister Sussan Ley that any cuts to the ancillary rebate will only hit consumers.
TEXT:
Health funds have warned their minister Sussan Ley that any cuts to the ancillary rebate will only hit consumers.

On Wednesday Ms Ley launched a nationwide review into private health insurance to run alongside reviews into primary care and the Medicare Benefits Schedule.

She singled out the 30 per cent rebate on ancillaries, which includes things like dental, glasses, and physiotherapy, as a potential savings target. The rebate was part of a package of reforms introduced in 1999 to encourage people to take up private health cover.

"There are certainly questions that need to be asked, such as perhaps the ancillary model would be better directed to encourage Australian to save for their out of pocket primary care expenses," Ms Ley said.

Bupa health insurance managing director Dwayne Crombie said the question mark cast over ancillaries is a concern.

"They seem to have articulated a predisposition to eliminate the ancillary rebate without stating whether they are looking to just save money or reprioritise its use to other worthwhile activities such as making hospital policies more affordable," Mr Crombie said.

"Given 12 million Australians receive this rebate there could be a lot of unintended consequences to consumers."

Dr Crombie said it is "critical" to get affordability under control to prevent systemic cover downgrades by price-conscious consumers.

"If consumers continue to downgrade or drop their health cover there will be serious knock-on effects for the whole system," he said.

Between 85 to 90 cents from each dollar spent on premiums is paid to healthcare providers. Last year more than $17 billion was spent on private health treatments.

Bupa is Australia's second biggest private health insurer covering just over 3.9 million Australians. Mark Fitzgibbon, who heads listed health insurer nib, said he thought any talk of cutting the rebate was "nonsense" because "this is not the time to be tampering with the rebate".

He said government spending cannot simply be passed onto insurers because it ended up boosting premiums for private health policies.

"When the government ended its dental program for people with chronic diseases [2012] that happened very suddenly and shifted about $100 million in costs from the taxpayer to private health insurance policyholders," he said. "I think the biggest risk [with the federal review] is that we don't properly model the funding shift from public to private."

The health funds also said prostheses must be a key focal point for the review, pointing to excessive costs and price discrepancies.

Medibank Private managing director George Savvides said that over the last three years benefits for prostheses have, on average, grown by 8.6 per cent a year.

In 2013-14 health insurers paid $1.75 billion for prosthesis items, around 14 per cent of total outlays.

"We spend more on prosthetic devices now than we do on doctors. The cost variation is just outrageous, Mr Fitzgibbon said. We need a new system".

Key points

More than $17 billion was spent on private health treatments last year.

The 30 per cent rebate on ancillary items could be scrapped.
